Title: Ecological novelty induced by climate change | Nature Climate Change
Description: Climate change is altering the conditions experienced by organisms and ecosystems at a pace unprecedented on geological timescales. The resulting shifts in terrestrial and marine systems fall under the umbrella of ecological novelty, which describes the effects of rapid change at multiple scales. This Review explores the mechanisms behind climate change-induced ecological novelty and its manifestation across global biomes. We contextualize novelty within a deep time perspective of past climate shifts and ecological reorganization. We find ample evidence for the severe disruption of ecological communities from the direct and indirect effects of climate change, and novelty emerging through climate change adaptation and mitigation measures. Potential interventions fall along a gradient of managing against, tolerating or managing for ecological novelty. The authors review ecological novelty—ecological situations with no precedent—arising from climate change. They discuss ecological novelty due to direct and indirect effects of climate change, and due to adaptation and mitigation measures, and explore management options that are against, for or tolerant of ecological novelty.

Title: Unifying bright spots research for people and nature | Nature Ecology & Evolution
Description: Understanding how systems thrive against the odds is increasingly important in an era of accelerating ecological and social change. Bright spots, cases that outperform expectations under local constraints, offer a lens for learning from success within broader patterns of decline. Yet progress in this field has been limited by inconsistent definitions, fragmented methods and the absence of an integrative framework for systematic learning and application. Here we synthesize more than 70 studies spanning ecology, conservation, resource use, food production and sustainability science to assess how bright spots are identified, interpreted and applied in research, policy and practice. We introduce a typology of six approaches for identifying bright spots, highlighting their assumptions, strengths and trade-offs. We distil enabling conditions associated with bright spots, grouped into specific practices and processes, social capacities and context. Building on this synthesis, we develop a unifying framework that moves bright spots research from isolated case studies towards a coherent and cumulative understanding of how unexpected success can be identified, interpreted and compared across systems. By uncovering conditions under which systems exceed expectations, bright spots research reveals where unexpected success happens, why, and how to replicate it in an era of accelerating social–ecological change. This Review presents a typology for how to identify and interpret bright spots, or positive deviance, in conservation and sustainability science—cases where unexpectedly positive outcomes occur despite local constraints.

Title: Functional capacities drive recruitment of bacteria into plant root microbiota | Nature Microbiology
Description: Root-associated microbiomes are shaped by the plant, yet vary across environments and hosts, challenging prediction and engineering. Here, to uncover principles of bacterial selection at the root–soil interface, we applied a systems-level approach using reconstitution studies with communities of isolates from Arabidopsis, barley and Lotus grown in soil. Functional divergence among the microbiota of the host plants reflected distinct strategies: in Arabidopsis and barley, recruitment was primarily shaped by inoculum, while Lotus root environment favoured fewer, functionally diverse isolates, akin to a ‘Swiss army knife’ strategy. Despite taxonomic variability, root microbiomes encoded overlapping functions. Across major taxa, isolates with broad but distinct functional repertoires within their families were consistently more abundant. Using a genome-to-function framework that is function centric, taxonomically inclusive and host-context aware, we identified 266 functions enriched across all root microbiomes. This functional backbone emerged as a core signature of plant-associated bacteria, providing a solid foundation for microbiome engineering in agriculture. Functional versatility plays a key role in shaping root microbiota.

Title: Net transfer of carbon between ectomycorrhizal tree species in the field | Nature
Description: Different plant species can be compatible with the same species of mycorrhizal fungi1,2 and be connected to one another by a common mycelium3,4. Transfer of carbon3,4,5, nitrogen6,7 and phosphorus8,9 through interconnecting mycelia has been measured frequently in laboratory experiments, but it is not known whether transfer is bidirectional, whether there is a net gain by one plant over its connected partner, or whether transfer affects plant performance in the field10,11. Laboratory studies using isotope tracers show that the magnitude of one-way transfer can be influenced by shading of ‘receiver’ plants3,5, fertilization of ‘donor’ plants with phosphorus12, or use of nitrogen-fixing donor plants and non-nitrogen-fixing receiver plants13,14, indicating that movement may be governed by source–sink relationships. Here we use reciprocal isotope labelling in the field to demonstrate bidirectional carbon transfer between the ectomycorrhizal tree species Betula papyrifera and Pseudotsuga menziesii, resulting in net carbon gain by P. menziesii. Thuja plicata seedlings lacking ectomycorrhizae absorb small amounts of isotope, suggesting that carbon transfer between B. papyrifera and P. menziesii is primarily through the direct hyphal pathway. Net gain by P. menziesii seedlings represents on average 6% of carbon isotope uptake through photosynthesis. The magnitude of net transfer is influenced by shading of P. menziesii, indicating that source–sink relationships regulate such carbon transfer under field conditions.

Title: Forest tree growth is linked to mycorrhizal fungal composition and function across Europe | The ISME Journal
Description: Most trees form symbioses with ectomycorrhizal fungi (EMF) which influence access to growth-limiting soil resources. Mesocosm experiments repeatedly show that EMF species differentially affect plant development, yet whether these effects ripple up to influence the growth of entire forests remains unknown. Here we tested the effects of EMF composition and functional genes relative to variation in well-known drivers of tree growth by combining paired molecular EMF surveys with high-resolution forest inventory data across 15 European countries. We show that EMF composition was linked to a three-fold difference in tree growth rate even when controlling for the primary abiotic drivers of tree growth. Fast tree growth was associated with EMF communities harboring high inorganic but low organic nitrogen acquisition gene proportions and EMF which form contact versus medium-distance fringe exploration types. These findings suggest that EMF composition is a strong bio-indicator of underlying drivers of tree growth and/or that variation of forest EMF communities causes differences in tree growth. While it may be too early to assign causality or directionality, our study is one of the first to link fine-scale variation within a key component of the forest microbiome to ecosystem functioning at a continental scale.

Description: The first of more than two dozen endangered monarch butterflies tagged with radio trackers on the Prairies this summer has made it to Mexico to overwinter, a mere five weeks after fluttering off from Winnipeg.

Title: Fijian bee genomics suggest 99% effective population decline since European colonization
Description: The decline of pollinator species due to habitat loss and pesticide use over recent decades has been a global concern. Pollinators like bees and butterflies support both wild plants and agricultural food production, but many species are threatened and remain poorly studied. It's estimated that bees, in particular, pollinate between 78% and 94% of all plant species.

Title: Spatially organized chemical defences shape microbial communities in honey bee colonies
Description: The diversity, redundancy, and spatial arrangement of these defences suggest that antimicrobial activity is not the property of any single material but may instead arise from their coordinated deployment across the colony.

Title: Mosquito repellency mediated by skin commensal Bacillus species via volatile metabolite reprogramming | Nature Communications
Description: Individual variation in human attractiveness to mosquitoes critically influences vector-borne disease transmission, and this phenomenon arises from multiple underlying factors. This study integrated human skin microbiome profiling, non-human primate in situ intervention, and volatilomics to uncover a microbial-mediated mechanism underlying host-specific mosquito repellency. Bacillus species were identified as a microbial signature associated with reduced mosquito attraction in humans. Targeted Intervention of B. licheniformis and B. paralicheniformis on primate skin was sufficient to significantly reduce mosquito attraction, thereby establishing a causal microbial contribution beyond descriptive correlations. Mechanistic analyses revealed that Bacillus enrichment reprogrammed the skin volatilome, specifically increasing the abundance of aromatic and fatty acid-derived effectors, such as p-Cresol and decanoic acid, which are associated with repellency phenotypes. Together, these findings revealed a potential role of skin commensals in shaping mosquito host-seeking behavior, providing a molecular basis for microbiome-informed and bio-inspired strategies for mosquito disease control. Why some people get bitten by mosquitoes more than others has been a long-standing question. Here, the authors uncover specific chemical compounds produced by two resident skin microbes that, when applied to animals, reduce their “attractiveness” to mosquitoes and increases repellent time.
